newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond and interest rate futures confounded predictions they would slide if Socialist-led government, including the Communists, won in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Traders said they had expected a sharp selloff on the result, but when prices were marked sharply lower at the open, non-resident and domestic investors alike stepped in to close positions set up to take advantage of a slump.
Short covering sent bond and interest rate futures well into positive territory, but analysts warned the move may be overdone given the risks to the EMU process ahead.
A larger than expected rise in the U.S. May national purchasing managers index (NAPM), partly offset by a drop in the price component capped the bond future's gains.

The June bond future settled up 0.02 at 128.52 after touching a low of 127.86 in pre-session electronic trading. It reached a high of 127.78, closing a gap on daily charts left since May 22, before the first round of voting on May 25.

June PIBOR, expected to be the most sensitive to an election surprise, had a similarly volatile day. It slumped to 96.15 in the GLOBEX session before rallying to a high of 96.45, also filling a gap left on charts from May 23.

Analysts said while the consensus seemed to be that a left-wing government would not derail a single European currency, even with the anti-Maastricht Communists in the government, some domestic investors remained cautious.

"Our traders are not seeing any selling of any description but our sales force are saying they haven't seen any cash buyers. The domestic investors are very nervous and are sitting on their hands," a bond analyst at a French bank said.
"Lots of people were astonished by the lack of negative reaction and we've seen huge short covering," a futures trader at a French brokerage said.

The initial slide sent the 10-year spread between French and German yields into minus three basis but it was back at minus 10 late in the session, down from minus 15 on Friday, and little changed since the snap election was called on April 21.

Analysts said the concerns about a row between the German government and the Bundesbank over the revaluation of gold reserves in 1997, designed to help German reduce its debt level, had partly taken the sting out of the French decline.
Rather than sell France alone, investors were more keen on avoiding Europe until there was a clearer picture of whether EMU would be delayed, or go ahead with a large number of countries.

"A lot of people had taken bearish French positions. Now people are caught between strategies of EMU delay or a regrouping of core around a softer intepretation," Mark Capelton, international economist at BZW said. "It adds weight to the sell Europe story, but not France against Germany."
A bond trader said it was all very well wanting to sell France but given it was not that clear what else to buy in Europe. "It's a draw between France and Germany."
"The German situation is advantageous for the franc," which in turn was helping the bond and interest rate futures, a futures trader said.

Widespread selling of the mark against other major non-European currencies saved the French franc from a sustained attack. The French unit fell as low as 3.3860, a six-month low, but then rallied as high as 3.3700 as the German currency fell.

"The franc might be sold against the dollar, sterling or yen but not against the mark. The franc and the mark both have moved in the same direction against the dollar since this morning," Francois Chevallier, economist at Credit National-BFCE said.
